specAnchors.text: know the trend in colour, boiling point and viscosity of the main fractions
know that crude oil is a mixture of hydrocarbons
describe how the industrial process of fractional distillation separates crude oil into fractions
know the names and uses of the main fractions obtained from crude oil: refinery gases, gasoline, kerosene, diesel, fuel oil and bitumen

primer.text: From Classifying Organic Reactions you already know the three reaction types organic molecules undergo. This note meets the raw material they come from: crude oil, the column that sorts it, the six fractions worth learning by name, and the trends in their properties you must be able to explain.

modules.title: The mixture and the column that sorts it
modules.opening: Crude oil straight from the ground is a useless jumble, yet its separated parts power the world. This lesson follows the mixture into the fractionating column and explains why each group of molecules leaves where it does.
keyPoints: Crude oil is a mixture of hydrocarbons, which makes the crude itself of little direct use.
The useful groups inside it are called fractions, each containing hydrocarbons of similar chain lengths.
Fractional distillation separates the fractions because molecules of similar chain length have similar boiling points.
Crude oil is heated so it vaporises, and the vapours enter a fractionating column that is hot at the bottom and cooler at the top.
Vapours with high boiling points condense low down the column, while those with lower boiling points rise before condensing near the top.

low.restatement: Crude oil is a jumble of hydrocarbon molecules. Heating turns it to vapour, and inside a tall column that is hot below and cool above, each group condenses at the height matching its boiling point. Each group of similar molecules settles at its own level.
low.analogy: It is like a climbing wall where climbers rest at the height matching their strength: the weakest climbers of all rise to the cool top, and the strongest barely leave the hot ground.
low.examPointer: Tie every statement to the temperature gradient: hot bottom, cool top, condensation height set by boiling point.

medium.restatement: Crude oil is a mixture of hydrocarbons whose fractions are groups of similar chain length and therefore similar boiling points. In the industrial process the oil is heated until it vaporises, the vapours rise up a fractionating column with a temperature gradient, high-boiling vapours condense at the hot bottom, and low-boiling vapours climb to condense near the cool top.
medium.analogy: Picture a multi-storey car park with the busiest, heaviest vehicles parking on the ground floor and lighter ones driving freely to the top deck; boiling point plays the role of vehicle weight here.
medium.examPointer: Quote the two halves of the mechanism, vaporise then condense, and name the gradient direction when explaining why a fraction leaves at a given height.

modules.title: The main fractions and their trends
sourceHeadings: Properties of the main fractions of crude oil
Trend in boiling point of the main fractions
modules.opening: Six fractions carry names and uses you must memorise, and their properties line up in a strict order. This lesson walks the ladder from refinery gas to bitumen and explains every step of the trend.
keyPoints: The six main fractions run from refinery gases and gasoline through kerosene and diesel to fuel oil and bitumen.
Refinery gases serve domestic heating and cooking, gasoline fuels cars, and kerosene flies jets.
Diesel runs diesel engines, fuel oil powers ships and stations, and bitumen surfaces roads and roofs.
As chain length grows, boiling point and viscosity rise while the colour darkens and volatility falls.
The boiling point ladder runs from below 25 degrees for refinery gas to above 350 degrees for bitumen.

low.restatement: Going down the fraction ladder the chains get longer. Boiling points and thickness climb, the liquids get darker and less eager to evaporate, and the uses move from cooking gas to road tar. Bigger molecules attract each other more strongly, which is what drives every one of these trends.
low.analogy: It is like a row of syrups on a shelf: thin and pale at one end, thick and black at the other, with everything in between graded in the same direction.
low.examPointer: Learn the six names with one use each; the pairing is examinable word for word.

medium.restatement: Refinery gas, gasoline, kerosene, diesel, fuel oil and bitumen run from tiny chains boiling below room temperature to giant chains boiling above 350 degrees. Increasing chain length raises the attraction between molecules, so boiling point and viscosity climb, colour darkens, and volatility drops as bigger molecules hold on tighter and escape less easily.
medium.analogy: The fractions behave like pages of a sticker album from thin loose singles to a thick bound volume: the more material stuck together, the harder it is to pull one piece away or get the whole thing flowing.
medium.examPointer: Explain each trend through intermolecular attraction growing with molecular size, and anchor the argument with the carbon ranges from the table.

modules.title: Why the fractions matter beyond the column
sourceHeadings: What are the fractions used for?
modules.opening: Separated fractions feed transport, heating and the petrochemical industry at large. This lesson gathers the uses into one picture and explains why carbon chemistry can support such a variety of products.
keyPoints: Most modern transport runs on oil products, from cars and trains to aircraft.
Polymers, lubricants, solvents, detergents and adhesives are all obtained from crude oil.
The industry that turns oil into products underpins modern society and its development.
Carbon bonds strongly and repeatedly to itself, which lets it build a huge number of organic compounds.
The spread of fractions and their many products both stem from that bonding versatility of carbon.

low.restatement: Fractions fuel vehicles and aircraft, and feed factories making plastics, lubricants, solvents, detergents and adhesives. All of this variety comes from carbon bonding strongly to itself in many ways. Every product list you know, from petrol to glue, traces back to that one bonding ability.
low.analogy: Carbon is a master building brick: one brick type, endless models, which is why one barrel of oil supplies both the fuel and the plastic dashboard.
low.examPointer: Quote at least two non-fuel products, such as polymers and solvents, when asked about the importance of oil.

medium.restatement: The petrochemical industry underpins modern transport and manufacturing: cars, trains and aircraft burn oil-based fuels, while polymers, lubricants, solvents, detergents and adhesives come from the same crude feedstock. The range exists because carbon bonds strongly and repeatedly to itself, generating a huge number of distinct organic compounds.
medium.analogy: Crude oil is a combined petrol station and hardware store: the same tank fills the car and stocks the glue, the detergent and the plastic trim, all because carbon chains can be built to any specification.
medium.examPointer: Link the breadth of products to carbon bonding in your answer; the phrase strong covalent bonds with itself is the marking idea.

glossary.definition: Separating a liquid mixture by boiling and condensing, using differences in boiling points.
A group of hydrocarbons of similar chain length, and therefore similar boiling points, separated from crude oil.
The tall industrial tower, hot at the bottom and cooler at the top, in which crude oil fractions separate.
A measure of how easily a liquid flows; high viscosity liquids are thick and flow slowly.
The tendency of a substance to turn into vapour; volatile liquids evaporate easily.
